title: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
summary: Secure the path from commit to cloud: pipeline threat models, runners, tokens and OIDC, caches, Terraform plans and state, scanners, OPA and Sentinel policy, drift, with CircleCI and Ultralytics.
outcomes: Threat-model a CI/CD pipeline and spot direct, indirect and public poisoned pipeline execution
Isolate runners and cut pipeline credentials to least privilege with permissions, environments and OIDC
Write an exact OIDC trust for a deploy role and explain why wildcard subjects fail
Explain how caches and state files carry attacks, using Ultralytics, CircleCI and real state leaks
Review a Terraform plan and scan IaC and workflows with Checkov, Trivy and zizmor
Write and roll out Rego policy on plan JSON with enforcement levels and expiring exceptions
Detect drift with scheduled plans and choose between reverting and codifying a change

lessons.title: DevSecOps: security checks on the path from commit to cloud

blocks.md:
Start with one small change. A developer edits a Terraform file so a server accepts SSH from anywhere, opens a pull request, a teammate approves it, and twenty minutes later the rule is live in production. No human typed a command into the cloud console: a pipeline did everything. That pipeline is the subject of this course.

**DevOps** joins development and operations: the people who write software also ship and run it, through automation. **DevSecOps** (NIST spells it out as Development, Security and Operations, in [SP 800-204C](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/204/c/final)) adds security to the same automated path, so checks run on every change instead of in a review at the end. Recall from the supply chain course that **CI/CD** (continuous integration and continuous delivery or deployment) is the machinery that builds, tests and ships every change.

NIST SP 800-204C, a US government guide to DevSecOps, divides the code behind a modern application into types that include **application code**, **infrastructure as code** (IaC: servers, networks and permissions described in files and created by a tool) and **policy as code** (rules written as files that a program evaluates). This course works on two of those types, plus the pipeline that applies them:

- **Pipeline code**: the workflow files that say what CI runs, when, and with which credentials.
- **Infrastructure as code**: Terraform, AWS CloudFormation templates and Helm charts (packages of Kubernetes manifests).
- **Policy as code**: rules in Rego or Sentinel that decide whether a change may go ahead.

Each is code, so each can be reviewed, tested and versioned. Each can also be attacked.

Why attackers care: the pipeline is usually the most privileged identity in a company. It can publish packages, assume deployment roles and change production. Whoever controls what the pipeline runs gets all of that, without ever logging in to the cloud.

**OWASP** (Open Worldwide Application Security Project, a nonprofit that publishes free security guidance) keeps a [Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-ci-cd-security-risks/) list, numbered CICD-SEC-1 to 10: insufficient flow control, inadequate identity and access management, dependency chain abuse, poisoned pipeline execution, insufficient pipeline-based access controls, insufficient credential hygiene, insecure system configuration, ungoverned third-party services, improper artifact integrity validation, and insufficient logging and visibility. The supply chain course covered dependencies and artifact integrity. This course goes deep on PPE, access controls, credential hygiene and configuration, and touches flow control, identity, third-party services and logging.

blocks.title: The delivery path, and where security checks sit

scenes.caption: The path every change takes: a developer opens a pull request, CI runs on it, a reviewer approves, the deploy job applies the change to the cloud.
The attack points. The PR carries untrusted content, the runner executes it, secrets sit in the deploy job, and the state file describes every resource.
The checks this course adds: scanners and policy on the PR, a protected environment before deploy, and short-lived OIDC credentials instead of stored keys.
After deploy, a scheduled drift check compares the cloud with the code, because console changes never pass through the pipeline.

blocks.md: The pipeline is a privileged identity. Its definition files, its runners, its credentials and its state files deserve the same protection as production, because each one is a path into production.

How the course runs: lessons 2 to 7 secure the pipeline (who can make it run code, where that code runs, which credentials it holds, and two real breaches). Lessons 8 to 10 review infrastructure as code and the state file. Lessons 11 and 12 write policy as code and roll it out without stopping developers. Lesson 13 catches drift, and lesson 14 assembles everything into one pipeline with a response plan.

blocks.question: A company locks down its cloud console with MFA and short sessions, but its deploy pipeline holds a long-lived admin key. Where should an attacker aim?
options: At the console, because it holds the most permissions
At the pipeline: anyone who can make it run their code inherits its admin key without touching the console
At the developer's laptop only, since pipelines cannot be attacked
Nowhere: MFA on the console protects every path into the account
blocks.explain: Console MFA protects one door. The pipeline is another identity with the same or more power, and it acts on code it is given. Controlling its input or its runner is as good as owning its key.

blocks.question: Which item is policy as code?
options: A Terraform file that creates an S3 bucket
A GitHub Actions workflow that runs unit tests
A Rego file stating that no security group may allow SSH from 0.0.0.0/0
A wiki page listing the company's security standards
blocks.explain: Policy as code is a rule a machine evaluates. The Terraform file is infrastructure as code, the workflow is pipeline code, and a wiki page is policy that nobody's pipeline can enforce.

lessons.title: Threat-modelling a pipeline: poisoned pipeline execution

blocks.md:
Threat-model a pipeline the way the threat modelling course taught: draw the data flow, then mark trust boundaries. The key question for a pipeline is short: **who can make it run code they wrote, and with which credentials in reach?**

A tiny example. A repository has a workflow that runs `make test` on every push to every branch, and the AWS deploy key is a repository secret available to that workflow. Anyone who can push a branch, which is every engineer and anyone holding a stolen engineer session, can make the pipeline run code next to that key.

OWASP calls this **poisoned pipeline execution** (PPE, CICD-SEC-4): someone with access to source control, but not to the build environment, gets the pipeline to run their commands ([OWASP PPE](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-ci-cd-security-risks/CICD-SEC-04-Poisoned-Pipeline-Execution)). It names three forms:

- **Direct PPE (D-PPE)**: the attacker edits the CI configuration file itself on a branch or in a PR, and the pipeline runs it.
- **Indirect PPE (I-PPE)**: the CI file is protected, so the attacker edits a file the CI file calls: a Makefile, a test, a script, a linter's config.
- **Public PPE (3PE)**: in a public repository, an anonymous outsider does the same through a pull request. The supply chain course's pwn requests are this case.

blocks.code:
# Vulnerable: every push to every branch runs repo code with deploy keys
name: ci
on: push
jobs:
  build-and-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}
      AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - run: make test            # Makefile comes from the pushed branch
      - run: make deploy
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
blocks.caption: Vulnerable. The `if:` only guards the deploy step; the keys are in the job's environment for `make test` too, and the Makefile is whatever the pushed branch says. That is I-PPE from any branch.

blocks.code:
# Fixed: untrusted work has no credentials; deploy needs main plus approval
name: ci
on: push
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest           # no secrets, no cloud identity
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - run: make test
  deploy:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production          # branch rule: main only; required reviewers
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write                # OIDC: no stored AWS key at all
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@e1253824e5c10ff9df46874f81ed3ec929e19cfd # v6.3.0
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/shop-deploy
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - run: make deploy
blocks.caption: Fixed. The test job, which runs branch code, holds nothing worth stealing. The deploy job can only start from main and only after a reviewer approves the production environment, and the AWS role trusts that environment only (lesson 6).

blocks.title: I-PPE from a stolen engineer session, before and after the fix

scenes.caption: An attacker with a stolen engineer session pushes a branch that changes only the Makefile. The workflow file is untouched, so a review of CI files would see nothing.
The push triggers the vulnerable workflow. The runner checks out the branch and runs make test with the AWS keys already in its environment.
The modified Makefile sends the keys out. Nothing failed, so the run is green.
With the fix, the same push runs the test job with no secrets: the attacker's code runs but finds nothing to send.
The deploy job never starts for this branch: the production environment allows main only and waits for a reviewer.

blocks.md: Protecting the workflow file is not enough. With I-PPE the attacker never touches it: they edit what it calls. Treat everything the privileged job executes (Makefiles, scripts, test files, tool configs, lockfiles) as part of the pipeline.

**Defender view.**

- **Prevent**: split jobs by trust. Code from branches and PRs runs without secrets; credentials live only in jobs that run reviewed code from protected branches. Put `.github/workflows/` and build scripts under **CODEOWNERS** (a GitHub file naming the reviewers who must approve changes to given paths), as GitHub's [secure use reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use) suggests. Protect main with a ruleset (branch rules): require a pull request with an approval and passing checks, and block force pushes, so "from main" really means reviewed code.
- **Detect**: audit logs for new branches followed by workflow runs that touch secrets; runs on non-default branches that use deploy credentials; outbound connections from runners to unknown hosts (lesson 3).
- **Respond**: treat every secret the job could read as stolen, rotate it, and review what the identity did.

blocks.question: A team stores the pipeline definition in a separate repository that only the platform team can edit. The pipeline runs `npm test` on every developer branch with a registry token in the environment. Are they safe from PPE?
options: No: this is the indirect form. Anyone who can push a branch can change package.json scripts or test files that npm test runs
Yes, because the CI file cannot be edited by developers
Yes, as long as the token is masked in logs
No, but only if the repository is public
blocks.explain: OWASP lists exactly this as I-PPE: the CI config is protected, but files it executes are not. Masking only hides values in logs; code that runs can still send the token anywhere.

blocks.question: In the fixed workflow, why does the deploy job also need the production environment, when it already has `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`?
options: The `if:` is cosmetic and GitHub ignores it
Environments make jobs run faster
The `if:` lives in the workflow file, which a branch can edit; the environment's branch rule and reviewers are enforced by GitHub outside the file, and the cloud role can require that environment
Environments are needed to use actions/checkout
blocks.explain: A condition written in the workflow is only as trustworthy as the file. A branch can delete it. Environment protection rules are settings the branch cannot change, and an OIDC trust on environment:production means the cloud refuses tokens from any other job.

lessons.title: Runners: where pipeline code runs, and how to isolate it

blocks.md:
A **runner** is the machine that executes a job. Whatever runs there, your build tool, a third-party action, an attacker's test file, shares that machine with every secret and token the job was given. So the first isolation question is: what else is on this machine, and what was on it before?

GitHub offers two kinds. **GitHub-hosted runners** are, in GitHub's words, "ephemeral and clean isolated virtual machines": a fresh VM per job, thrown away afterwards, so nothing persists between jobs. Inside that VM the job user has **passwordless sudo** ([GitHub-hosted runners](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/runners/github-hosted-runners)), meaning any step can become root. **Self-hosted runners** are machines you register yourself; GitHub's [secure use reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use) warns they have no guarantee of being clean, "can be persistently compromised by untrusted code", and "should almost never be used for public repositories".

**PyTorch, 2023.** Security researchers John Stawinski and Adnan Khan reported this chain to Meta's bug bounty on 9 August 2023 ([write-up](https://johnstawinski.com/2024/01/11/playing-with-fire-how-we-executed-a-critical-supply-chain-attack-on-pytorch/)):

1. PyTorch used **non-ephemeral** self-hosted runners: a process started by one job outlived it, and later jobs ran on the same machine.
2. The repository used GitHub's default fork setting, which asks for approval only for first-time contributors. They became contributors by getting a typo fix merged.
3. A pull request from their fork then ran a workflow on those runners without approval, and they installed persistence.
4. Privileged workflows later ran on those machines. actions/checkout keeps the GITHUB_TOKEN in `.git/config` during a job, so a write-scoped token could be read from disk; they also reached release secrets, including AWS keys and personal access tokens.

Meta paid USD 5,000 plus 10% for the delay. Their advice: require approval for all outside collaborators, and run fork PRs only on isolated, ephemeral runners.

blocks.title: Persistent vs ephemeral runners: what the release job inherits

scenes.caption: Persistent runner. A fork PR job runs at t=0 to 10 and starts a background process that outlives the job.
At t=30 a release job lands on the same machine with a write token and secrets. The leftover process reads them from disk and memory.
Ephemeral (just-in-time) runners. The same fork PR job runs on VM A, which is destroyed when the job ends.
The release job gets a brand-new VM B. Nothing from the PR job survived, so there is nothing waiting for the secrets.

blocks.md:
**Hardening self-hosted runners**, from GitHub's secure use reference:

- Use **just-in-time (JIT) runners**: created through the REST API, each "perform[s] at most one job before being automatically removed". GitHub notes that destroying a runner after each job by your own automation is weaker, because nothing guarantees a runner ran only one job.
- Put runners in **runner groups** and restrict which repositories may use each group. An organisation-level runner can otherwise receive jobs from many repositories.
- Keep untrusted work (PRs) and privileged work (releases, deploys) on different runners, and keep no long-lived keys on the machine itself.

**tj-actions, seen from the runner.** The supply chain course told how the action's tags were moved in March 2025. What the payload did on each runner is the isolation lesson. StepSecurity, a CI security company, [found](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/harden-runner-detection-tj-actions-changed-files-action-is-compromised) that it downloaded a Python script and ran it with `sudo` to dump the memory of the runner's worker process, where the job's secrets are held, then printed matches to the build log, base64-encoded twice. Two facts made that work: the step could become root (passwordless sudo), and it could reach the internet to fetch the script. StepSecurity's Harden-Runner, a GitHub Action that monitors and can block a runner's network traffic, caught it because "an unexpected endpoint appeared in the network traffic".

blocks.code:
jobs:
  test:                          # untrusted code: GitHub-hosted, no secrets
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: make test
  release:
    runs-on:
      group: release-runners     # group restricted to this repository
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: step-security/harden-runner@1d88384fd173af6ecb012dfd0264a306b711241a # v2.22.4
        with:
          egress-policy: block           # only the hosts below are reachable
          allowed-endpoints: >
            github.com:443
            pypi.org:443
            upload.pypi.org:443
          disable-sudo-and-containers: true
      - run: make release
blocks.caption: A release job on a restricted runner group, with a Harden-Runner egress (outbound traffic) allowlist and sudo blocked: that would have stopped the tj-actions payload. Caveat: the free tier covers only public repos on GitHub-hosted runners; on self-hosted runners it is a no-op without the paid tier.

blocks.md: Egress control is a strong layer (Harden-Runner is free only for public repositories; a self-hosted runner can use your own firewall): most CI theft needs either to download a second stage or to send data out. A build that may only talk to your registry and package index fails loudly when something else tries. Start in audit mode to learn the normal endpoints, then switch to block.

blocks.question: A team runs self-hosted runners and adds a script that wipes and re-images each VM after a job finishes. GitHub's guidance says this is weaker than it looks. Why?
options: Re-imaging is too slow to matter
GitHub-hosted runners are never wiped either
Wiping removes the runner's registration token, which breaks the next job
Nothing guarantees the runner took only one job before the wipe, so a second job (possibly privileged) can still land on a dirty machine; JIT runners are registered for exactly one job
blocks.explain: The secure use reference says automatic destruction might not be as effective as intended because there is no way to guarantee a self-hosted runner only runs one job. A just-in-time runner is removed by GitHub after at most one job.

blocks.question: Which controls would have stopped the tj-actions payload from reading secrets on a GitHub-hosted runner, according to how it worked?
options: Masking secrets in the log
Running the job on a larger runner
Blocking egress and sudo, since the payload had to download its memory-dump script and run it as root
Pinning actions/checkout to a SHA
blocks.explain: Masking did not help because the payload base64-encoded the values twice. The payload needed network access to fetch memdump.py and root to read another process's memory. Pinning the compromised action itself would also have helped; pinning checkout does nothing.

lessons.title: Least-privilege pipeline credentials: tokens, environments, secrets

blocks.md:
List what a typical job carries. A **GITHUB_TOKEN**, created for the job: GitHub fetches an installation access token before the job starts, and it expires when the job finishes or hits its maximum lifetime ([GitHub](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/github_token)). **Secrets** at repository, organisation or environment level. Sometimes a cloud key or a registry token. Each is something a compromised step can use, so each should be as small as the job allows. OWASP files this under CICD-SEC-6, insufficient credential hygiene.

A tiny example: a workflow that only runs tests needs to read the code. If its token can also push to main and create releases, a poisoned test can do both.

blocks.code:
# Vulnerable: one broad token and every secret for every job
name: ci
on: push
permissions: write-all
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      NPM_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}
      DEPLOY_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KEY }}
    steps:
      - run: npm ci && npm test
blocks.caption: Vulnerable. `write-all` gives the token write access to the repository and more; both secrets reach the test job, which never needs them.

blocks.code:
# Fixed: nothing by default, then the least each job needs
name: ci
on: push
permissions: {}
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - run: npm ci && npm test
  publish:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: npm-release        # holds NPM_TOKEN as an environment secret
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@949feb2413d6458794dcd2491c4babbbce0c15c1 # v7.1.0
        with:
          registry-url: https://registry.npmjs.org
      - run: npm publish
        env:
          NODE_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}
blocks.caption: Fixed. `permissions: {}` at the top removes every permission, and each job asks for what it uses. The registry token is an environment secret, so only the publish job can read it, and only after the environment's rules pass. Better: npm trusted publishing (OIDC, lesson 6) removes NPM_TOKEN.

blocks.md:
**Environments** are GitHub's gate in front of a job ([deployments and environments](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/deployments-and-environments)). A job that names one must pass its **deployment protection rules** first:

- **Required reviewers**: up to six people or teams; one approval lets the job run. **Prevent self-reviews** stops the person who triggered the deployment approving it.
- **Wait timer**: a delay of 1 to 43,200 minutes.
- **Deployment branches and tags**: only matching refs (for example main) may use the environment.
- **Environment secrets**: available only to jobs that reference the environment, and not until a required reviewer approves.

By default administrators can bypass these rules; you can turn that off. On GitHub Free, Pro and Team plans, required reviewers and wait timers work only in public repositories; private repositories need GitHub Enterprise for them, and GitHub Free has no environment secrets in private repositories.

blocks.title: An environment secret reaches a job only after approval

scenes.caption: The publish job starts and names the npm-release environment. GitHub checks the branch rule first: main is allowed.
The environment requires a reviewer, so the job pauses. No secret has been sent to the runner yet.
The person who pushed the commit tries to approve their own deployment. With prevent self-reviews on, GitHub refuses.
A second maintainer approves. Only now does GitHub hand the environment secret to the job, which publishes.

blocks.md: GitHub's environment docs note that workflows on self-hosted runners are not run in an isolated container, even if they use environments. An environment controls when a secret is released, not what else on that machine can read it afterwards. Pair environments with clean runners (lesson 3).

**Log redaction is a safety net, not a control.** The runner replaces known secret values in logs with stars, but GitHub's secure use reference warns redaction "is not guaranteed": it works by exact match. So: never store structured data (a JSON blob of credentials) as one secret, register derived values (such as a JWT you sign with a secret) with `::add-mask::`, and if a secret does reach a log, delete the log and rotate the secret.

**Defender view.** Prevent: `permissions: {}` by default, environment secrets for anything that publishes or deploys, OIDC instead of stored keys (lesson 6). Detect: alert on secrets used from jobs or branches that should not have them, and review audit logs for changes to environment rules. Respond: rotate everything the job could reach.

blocks.question: A deploy key is stored as a JSON document with three fields in one secret. A tool prints the parsed `private_key` field on error. What happens in the log?
options: It is probably shown: redaction matches the exact stored string, and one field of the parsed JSON is a different string
It is masked, because the whole secret is masked
The job fails before printing
GitHub deletes the log automatically
blocks.explain: GitHub warns that structured data makes redaction fail because redaction largely relies on finding an exact match. Store each sensitive value as its own secret.

blocks.question: A maintainer sets required reviewers on the production environment and lists themselves as the only reviewer. They push a change and approve its deployment. Which setting would have forced a second person?
options: Wait timer
Deployment branches
Prevent self-reviews
Allow administrators to bypass
blocks.explain: With prevent self-reviews enabled, users who initiate a deployment cannot approve it even if they are a required reviewer, so a deployment always involves two people. A wait timer only delays it.

lessons.title: CircleCI 2023: when the platform holding your secrets is breached

blocks.md:
Every lesson so far assumed the CI service itself is trustworthy. It is also a company, with employees, laptops and databases full of its customers' secrets. If you store a cloud key in a hosted CI service, your key is now protected by their security as well as yours.

CircleCI is a hosted CI/CD service. Its CTO (chief technology officer), Rob Zuber, published the [incident report](https://circleci.com/blog/jan-4-2023-incident-report/) on 12 January 2023. All dates below are from it.

**What happened.**

1. **16 December 2022**: malware on an engineer's laptop, missed by antivirus, stole a valid single sign-on session already backed by 2FA. With the session cookie, the attacker needed neither password nor second factor.
2. The engineer could generate production access tokens as part of their job, so the attacker escalated into a subset of production systems. Reconnaissance followed on **19 December**.
3. **22 December**: exfiltration from databases and stores holding customer environment variables, tokens and keys. The data was encrypted at rest, but the attacker "extracted encryption keys from a running process".
4. **29 December**: a customer reported suspicious GitHub OAuth activity. CircleCI began rotating all customers' GitHub OAuth tokens on 31 December.
5. **4 January 2023**: the account was shut off, production access cut, hosts rotated, and customers told to rotate every secret. API tokens were revoked on 5 and 6 January.

When the report was published, fewer than 5 customers had told CircleCI of unauthorised access to third-party systems.

scenes.caption: Day 0 (16 Dec): the laptop is compromised and the SSO session stolen. Days 3 to 6: reconnaissance, then customer secrets copied on day 6 (22 Dec).
Day 13 (29 Dec): a customer spots odd GitHub OAuth use. Day 15: CircleCI starts rotating GitHub OAuth tokens, a job that ran until day 22.
Day 19 (4 Jan): access cut and disclosure; days 20 and 21: API tokens revoked. Every customer secret was exposed for at least 13 days before customers could act.

blocks.md: Encryption at rest did not save the secrets, because a running service must decrypt them to use them, and the attacker read the keys from a running process. The only secret a breached CI vendor cannot leak is one it never stored.

**What CircleCI told customers to do next**, in its own best-practices list: use **OIDC tokens** wherever possible "to avoid storing long-lived credentials in CircleCI"; use **IP ranges** so your systems accept connections only from known addresses; use **contexts** (named groups of secrets) to restrict which projects can read which secrets; and use self-hosted **runners** when you need your own network and IAM controls.

For a defender responding to such a vendor breach, the report gives the window to search: activity from 16 December 2022 to the date you finished rotating, plus indicators such as unexpected `repo.download_zip` events in GitHub audit logs. After customer feedback, CircleCI also released a script that finds the secrets a customer had stored, to give an actionable list for rotation.

blocks.code:
from datetime import date

# Secrets stored in the CI platform: (name, kind, last rotated)
inventory = [
    ("AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID", "cloud key", date(2022, 3, 2)),
    ("NPM_TOKEN", "registry token", date(2022, 11, 20)),
    ("DEPLOY_SSH_KEY", "ssh key", date(2023, 1, 6)),
    ("SLACK_WEBHOOK", "webhook", date(2021, 7, 14)),
    ("AWS_ROLE_ARN", "role ARN (OIDC)", None),  # not a secret: no key stored
]
safe_after = date(2023, 1, 5)   # CircleCI: entered after this, secure

for name, kind, rotated in inventory:
    if rotated is None:
        verdict = "nothing to rotate"
    elif rotated <= safe_after:
        verdict = "ROTATE, then audit its use since 2022-12-16"
    else:
        verdict = "already rotated after the all-clear"
    print(f"{name:<18} {kind:<16} {verdict}")
blocks.caption: A response helper: list what you stored in the CI platform and decide what to rotate, using CircleCI's statement that anything entered after 5 January 2023 can be considered secure. The inventory is made up; the dates are from the report.

blocks.code:
$ python3 rotate.py
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID  cloud key        ROTATE, then audit its use since 2022-12-16
NPM_TOKEN          registry token   ROTATE, then audit its use since 2022-12-16
DEPLOY_SSH_KEY     ssh key          already rotated after the all-clear
SLACK_WEBHOOK      webhook          ROTATE, then audit its use since 2022-12-16
AWS_ROLE_ARN       role ARN (OIDC)  nothing to rotate
blocks.caption: Real output. The OIDC row is the point: a role ARN identifies a role but grants nothing on its own, because AWS only issues credentials to a token signed by the CI provider with the right claims.

blocks.question: CircleCI encrypted customer secrets at rest. Why were they still exposed?
options: The encryption algorithm was broken
The attacker extracted the encryption keys from a running process, which must hold them to use the secrets
Secrets were stored in plain text by mistake
The customers' own laptops were compromised
blocks.explain: The report says data was encrypted at rest but keys were extracted from a running process. At-rest encryption protects stolen disks and backups, not a service that is running and compromised.

blocks.question: After a CI vendor breach, which kind of pipeline credential needs no rotation at all?
options: A long-lived cloud access key stored as a project secret
An SSH deploy key stored in the CI service
A registry token kept in a context
A cloud role assumed through OIDC, where the CI service stores only the role name
blocks.explain: With OIDC the CI service holds no long-lived secret: it presents a short-lived signed token each run. Stolen role names grant nothing. Every stored key or token must be rotated.

lessons.title: OIDC from CI, precisely: subject claims and environments

blocks.md:
The cloud security course showed the mechanism: the CI job gets a signed **OIDC** token (OpenID Connect, an identity layer on OAuth 2.0), and AWS swaps it for temporary credentials if the role's trust policy accepts the token's claims. The security lives entirely in that trust policy. This lesson is about writing its `sub` condition precisely.

The `sub` (subject) claim says which workflow context asked. GitHub builds it from metadata ([OIDC reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/oidc)), and the shape depends on the job:

- Job with an environment: `repo:ORG/REPO:environment:NAME`
- Pull request event (no environment): `repo:ORG/REPO:pull_request`
- Branch: `repo:ORG/REPO:ref:refs/heads/BRANCH`
- Tag: `repo:ORG/REPO:ref:refs/tags/TAG`

Order matters: if the job names an environment, the subject is the environment form, whatever the trigger.

AWS conditions compare strings. `StringEquals` needs an exact match. `StringLike` allows wildcards: `*` matches any run of characters, including `/` and `:`. A wildcard that looks harmless can accept far more than intended. Let us measure it on five tokens one organisation might produce.

blocks.code:
import re

def string_like(pattern, value):
    # IAM StringLike: * matches any run of characters, ? matches one
    rx = "".join(".*" if c == "*" else "." if c == "?" else re.escape(c)
                 for c in pattern)
    return re.fullmatch(rx, value) is not None

subjects = [
    "repo:example-org/shop-site:environment:production",
    "repo:example-org/shop-site:ref:refs/heads/main",
    "repo:example-org/shop-site:ref:refs/heads/test-branch",
    "repo:example-org/shop-site:pull_request",
    "repo:example-org/intern-sandbox:ref:refs/heads/main",
]
conditions = {
    "StringLike repo:example-org/*": lambda s: string_like("repo:example-org/*", s),
    "StringLike repo:example-org/shop-site:*": lambda s: string_like("repo:example-org/shop-site:*", s),
    "StringEquals ...:environment:production":
        lambda s: s == "repo:example-org/shop-site:environment:production",
}
for name, test in conditions.items():
    allowed = [s.split(":", 1)[1] for s in subjects if test(s)]
    print(f"{name}: {len(allowed)} of {len(subjects)} accepted")
    for a in allowed:
        print("   ", a)
blocks.caption: A model of IAM's StringLike matching (only * and ? are special) applied to five real-format GitHub subjects.

blocks.prompt: Before running it: which of the five subjects does `repo:example-org/shop-site:*` accept? It looks like it pins the repository.
blocks.reveal:
Four of five. It rejects only the other repository, but it accepts `test-branch` and `pull_request`, so anyone who can push any branch or open a same-repository PR gets the production role. It pins the repository and nothing else. Only the exact environment subject narrows the role to one gated job:

```
StringLike repo:example-org/*: 5 of 5 accepted
StringLike repo:example-org/shop-site:*: 4 of 5 accepted
StringEquals ...:environment:production: 1 of 5 accepted
```

blocks.title: How many of five tokens each trust condition accepts

scenes.caption: repo:example-org/* accepts all five tokens, including one from a different repository in the same organisation.
repo:example-org/shop-site:* still accepts four: every branch and every pull request in the repository.
An exact environment subject accepts one token: the job GitHub let into the production environment after its branch rule and reviewers.

blocks.md:
**The pattern that holds up:** pair an exact environment subject with environment protection rules. The cloud then trusts a job only if GitHub admitted it to the environment, and GitHub admits it only from main and after a reviewer approves. A branch that edits the workflow to call the role directly produces a `ref:refs/heads/...` subject and is refused.

Use two roles: a read-only **plan role** trusted for pull requests, so reviewers see a Terraform plan (lesson 8), and a write **apply role** trusted for `environment:production` only. Read-only is not harmless: plan must read the state, and every secret in it (lesson 9), so keep secrets out of state.

Two details from GitHub's reference. Colons inside values are encoded as `%3A`. And repositories created after 15 July 2026 use an immutable subject that includes owner and repository IDs, such as `repo:OWNER@OWNER-ID/REPO@REPO-ID:ref:refs/heads/BRANCH`, so a recreated repository with a recycled name cannot match old trust policies. Write the trust for the format your repository uses.

Ultralytics (next lesson) used PyPI trusted publishing, the same OIDC idea, without a GitHub environment. PyPI calls environments optional but recommended; William Woodruff's analysis notes that without one, compromising the workflow was enough to trigger a publish. PyPI adds that it did not matter this time: the poisoned cache rode inside releases the project triggered itself. A gate on a job context helps, but it cannot vet what the job reads.

blocks.question: A team's apply role trusts `StringLike` `repo:acme/infra:ref:refs/heads/*`. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: it pins the repository
It accepts tokens from other organisations
StringLike cannot be used with OIDC
It accepts tokens from every branch, so a pushed feature branch can assume the apply role
blocks.explain: The * matches any branch name. Trust the environment subject exactly, and let the environment's branch rule decide which branch may deploy.

blocks.question: A job runs on a pull_request event and references the environment `staging`. What subject does GitHub put in its token?
options: repo:ORG/REPO:pull_request
repo:ORG/REPO:ref:refs/pull/1/merge
repo:ORG/REPO:environment:staging
repo:ORG/REPO
blocks.explain: GitHub's reference: the subject includes the environment name when the job references an environment, and includes pull_request only if the job does not reference one.

lessons.title: Caches and artifacts: how Ultralytics was poisoned

blocks.md:
CI jobs reuse work through **caches**: a job saves a folder (downloaded pip packages, node_modules) under a key, usually a hash of the lockfile, and later jobs restore it instead of downloading again. `actions/setup-python` with `cache: pip` does this for you. Restoring a cache is extracting an archive into the job's working area, and GitHub's [caching reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/dependency-caching) is blunt: "Cache contents are not signed or verified", and extracted files "may modify files that are subsequently executed".

So a cache is a channel from whoever wrote it to whoever restores it. If a low-trust job can write a cache that a release job later restores, the low-trust job controls part of the release.

**The rules that decide who can read and write.** A run can restore caches from its own branch and from the default branch (and, for a PR, the base branch). Caches created by a `pull_request` run are scoped to the PR's merge ref, so they cannot reach main. The gap was other triggers that run *in the context of the default branch*, such as `pull_request_target` and `issue_comment`: they could write caches that main's release workflow would restore.

Adnan Khan's 2024 research ([The Monsters in Your Build Cache](https://adnanthekhan.com/2024/05/06/the-monsters-in-your-build-cache-github-actions-cache-poisoning/)) showed how to exploit that gap from a job with only a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN. Every job also receives a separate runtime token for GitHub's cache service, which Khan found stayed valid for 6 hours. Cache entries cannot be overwritten, but once a repository passes its 10 GB limit the least recently used entries are evicted, so filling the cache can free up a key to be written again.

**Ultralytics, December 2024.** Ultralytics is a popular Python package for computer-vision models. The chain comes from William Woodruff of Trail of Bits, a security research and consulting firm, who maintains the zizmor workflow linter ([analysis](https://blog.yossarian.net/2024/12/06/zizmor-ultralytics-injection)), and PyPI's [write-up](https://blog.pypi.org/posts/2024-12-11-ultralytics-attack-analysis/).

1. A `pull_request_target` workflow called a custom composite action (a reusable action made of a list of steps, here shell commands) that pasted the PR's branch name (`github.head_ref`) straight into a `git pull` shell command. Khan had reported a near-identical injection in August 2024; it was fixed, then reintroduced ten days later.
2. On 4 December an attacker opened a PR whose **branch name** was a shell command. The privileged workflow ran it.

What came next:

- The script read the runner's memory for the cache service token and URL. The analysis concludes the attacker very likely used them to plant a poisoned entry under the key of the release workflow's pip cache.
- The release workflow, running on main, restored the cache and built the package with a cryptocurrency miner inside. Versions 8.3.41 and 8.3.42 went to PyPI through the project's normal trusted publishing.
- Within about 36 hours, 8.3.45 and 8.3.46 appeared, uploaded directly with an old PyPI API token, still present in CI and probably stolen in the first round.

blocks.title: Ultralytics: from a branch name to a poisoned release

scenes.caption: The attacker opens a PR from a fork. The branch name itself contains a shell command.
The pull_request_target workflow runs in main's context and interpolates the branch name into a shell line. The command executes.
The script lifts the cache service token and URL from runner memory and sends them out.
With that token the attacker writes a poisoned entry under the key the release workflow's pip cache uses.
Later a push to main runs the release workflow. It restores the cache and builds the package with the miner included.
Round two skips CI: an old API token publishes 8.3.45 directly. With no matching attestation, this release looked different from the first.

blocks.md: **What helped responders.** Because Ultralytics used trusted publishing, the first malicious releases carried provenance attestations and entries in Sigstore's transparency log showing they came from the project's own workflow on main. That narrowed the search: the code was in the repository or injected during the build. The second round had no attestations and no matching repository activity, which pointed to a stolen token. PyPI's advice afterwards: avoid `pull_request_target` and shared caches in build and release workflows, revoke API tokens once trusted publishing works, and audit workflows with a tool such as zizmor.

blocks.code:
name: publish
on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  pypi:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: pypi
    permissions:
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-python@6d4fd22b20465ccc0f7354476588e8df7c9ca0e0 # v7.1.0
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
          cache: pip
      - run: python -m pip install build && python -m build
      - uses: pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@7245906fb61fa33a13554f9d5fb856fe61758086 # v1.14.3
blocks.caption: Vulnerable pattern. A tag-triggered publish job restores a pip cache. Every action is pinned and the job uses OIDC, yet whoever can write that cache key controls part of the release.

blocks.code:
$ zizmor --offline publish.yml
error[cache-poisoning]: runtime artifacts potentially vulnerable to a cache poisoning attack
  --> .github/workflows/publish.yml:17:9
   |
 2 | / on:
 3 | |   push:
 4 | |     tags: ["v*"]
   | |________________- generally used when publishing artifacts generated at runtime
...
17 |         - uses: actions/setup-python@6d4fd22b20465ccc0f7354476588e8df7c9ca0e0 # v7.1.0
   |           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ this step
...
20 |             cache: pip
   |             ---------- enables caching explicitly here

4 findings (3 suppressed): 0 informational, 0 low, 0 medium, 1 high
blocks.caption: Real zizmor 1.32.0 output, trimmed (note lines and a long underline shortened). zizmor is a static analyser for GitHub Actions workflows.

blocks.code:
pypi:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: pypi
    cache-mode: none               # this job neither restores nor saves caches
    permissions:
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-python@6d4fd22b20465ccc0f7354476588e8df7c9ca0e0 # v7.1.0
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"     # no cache: pip
      - run: python -m pip install build && python -m build
      - uses: pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@7245906fb61fa33a13554f9d5fb856fe61758086 # v1.14.3
blocks.caption: Fixed job. Release builds start from nothing: slower, but nothing a lower-trust job wrote can reach the artifact. zizmor then reports "No findings to report".

blocks.md:
**GitHub has since closed the default-branch gap.** Its caching reference now lists the only triggers that may create or overwrite caches in the default branch's scope (push, workflow_dispatch, repository_dispatch, delete, registry_package, page_build and schedule). Runs from other triggers that resolve to the default branch, including `pull_request_target`, `issue_comment` and `workflow_run`, get read-only access. A new `cache-mode` key (`read`, `write`, `write-only`, `none`) sets the least access a job needs; declaring `write` on a low-trust trigger switches the old risk back on.

**Artifacts have the same shape.** A `workflow_run` workflow that downloads artifacts uploaded by a PR workflow is reading attacker-controlled files. GitHub says such workflows "should treat artifacts uploaded from other workflows with caution": parse them as data, never execute them, and keep them away from secrets.

Anything a privileged job reads (a cache, an artifact, a downloaded tool, a config file) is part of its input. Ask who could have written it. If the answer includes a fork, a PR or a comment, the privileged job must treat it as untrusted data or not read it at all.

blocks.question: A pull_request_target workflow checks out PR code but has a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN and no secrets. Before GitHub's cache restrictions, what could still go wrong?
options: The PR code could use the job's cache token to write cache entries under main's scope, which a later release workflow would restore
Nothing: a read-only token cannot change anything
The PR could merge itself
The runner would crash
blocks.explain: This is exactly Adnan Khan's finding: the runtime cache token is separate from GITHUB_TOKEN. Writing into main's cache scope turned a low-privilege job into code inside the release.

blocks.question: Why could investigators tell that Ultralytics 8.3.45 was not built by the project's workflow?
options: Its version number was out of sequence
PyPI scans every upload for miners
It was larger than previous versions
It had no provenance attestation and no matching repository activity, unlike the releases from trusted publishing
blocks.explain: PyPI's write-up: the second round came from an unrevoked API token, which was detectable because there were no corresponding source repository activity or publish attestations.

lessons.title: Reviewing infrastructure as code: reading a Terraform plan

blocks.md:
Reviewing IaC means reviewing two things: the code a person wrote, and what the tool will actually do with it. For Terraform the second is the **plan**.

A quick refresher of the moving parts. Terraform (from HashiCorp, an infrastructure software company owned by IBM since 2025) reads files in **HCL** (HashiCorp Configuration Language) that declare **resources**, such as a security group. A **provider** is the plugin that talks to one platform's API (the `aws` provider calls AWS). Terraform keeps a **state** file recording which real objects it manages (lesson 9). `terraform plan` compares configuration, state and the live objects, and prints the changes it would make; `terraform apply` makes them.

The plan marks each resource with a symbol. These are from a real run on a toy configuration where one resource changed an input, one changed a value that forces a new object, and one was removed from the code:

blocks.code:
Terraform used the selected providers to generate the following execution
plan. Resource actions are indicated with the following symbols:
  ~ update in-place
  - destroy
-/+ destroy and then create replacement

  # terraform_data.cache will be updated in-place
  ~ resource "terraform_data" "cache" {
      ~ input  = "small" -> "large"
    }
  # terraform_data.db must be replaced
-/+ resource "terraform_data" "db" {
      ~ triggers_replace = "postgres-15" -> "postgres-16"
    }
  # terraform_data.old_queue will be destroyed
  # (because terraform_data.old_queue is not in configuration)
  - resource "terraform_data" "old_queue" {

Plan: 1 to add, 1 to change, 2 to destroy.
blocks.caption: Real Terraform 1.7.5 output, trimmed. `+` is create. A replacement counts as one add and one destroy, which is why 1 add appears with no new resource. For a real database, `-/+` means its data goes away.

blocks.md: The most dangerous line in a plan is often not an open port but a `-/+` or `-` on something stateful: a database, a bucket, a KMS key. Replacements are triggered by innocent-looking edits (a renamed resource, a changed engine version), and a reviewer skimming for security groups will miss them.
Now a security review of a real change. The file below adds a GitHub OIDC deploy role and a web security group. What would you flag?

blocks.caption: Two problems: SSH open to the whole internet, and a deploy role any repository in the organisation can assume (lesson 6). The provider block with dummy credentials used to produce the plans in this course is omitted.

blocks.md:
**A security reviewer's checklist for any plan:**

- **Identity**: new or changed roles, trust policies, policies with `*`, anything granting `iam:PassRole` or policy-editing rights.
- **Exposure**: `0.0.0.0/0`, public buckets or snapshots, public IPs, removed Block Public Access settings.
- **Data**: encryption turned off, keys scheduled for deletion, and every destroy or replace of something stateful.
- **Visibility**: logging, CloudTrail or flow logs disabled.
- **Supply chain**: new providers or modules, and changes to `.terraform.lock.hcl`, which pins provider versions and checksums.

Plans for real estates run to thousands of lines. Daniel Grzelak of Plerion, a cloud security company, points out that a person skimming such output on the hundredth run will not catch every odd line. So machines read the plan first, and people review what the machines flag.

blocks.code:
import json, sys

plan = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
RISKY_TYPES = {"aws_iam_role", "aws_iam_policy", "aws_iam_role_policy",
               "aws_security_group", "aws_s3_bucket_policy"}

for rc in plan["resource_changes"]:
    actions = rc["change"]["actions"]
    after = json.dumps(rc["change"]["after"] or {})
    notes = []
    if "delete" in actions:
        notes.append("DESTROYS or REPLACES an object")
    if rc["type"] in RISKY_TYPES:
        notes.append("identity or network change: human review")
    if "0.0.0.0/0" in after:
        notes.append("open to the whole internet")
    print(f'{"/".join(actions):<8} {rc["address"]:<24} {"; ".join(notes) or "-"}')

# terraform plan -out tfplan.binary
# terraform show -json tfplan.binary > tfplan.json
# python3 review_plan.py tfplan.json
blocks.caption: A minimal plan reader. `terraform show -json` turns the saved binary plan into JSON, whose `resource_changes` list holds each resource's actions and its before and after values.

blocks.code:
$ python3 review_plan.py tfplan.json          # the OIDC role and security group
create   aws_iam_role.deploy      identity or network change: human review
create   aws_security_group.web   identity or network change: human review; open to the whole internet

$ python3 review_plan.py p.json               # the toy plan above
update   terraform_data.cache     -
delete/create terraform_data.db        DESTROYS or REPLACES an object
delete   terraform_data.old_queue DESTROYS or REPLACES an object
blocks.caption: Real output on both plans. A replacement shows up as delete plus create in the JSON. The script cannot judge the wildcard in the trust policy; lesson 11 writes a precise rule for it.

blocks.title: What a plan is built from, and who reads it

scenes.caption: terraform plan reads three inputs: the HCL in the pull request, the state file, and the live objects in the cloud.
The binary plan is converted to JSON. That JSON, not the HCL, holds resolved values, such as a CIDR that came from a variable or a module.
Machines read the JSON first: scanners (lesson 10) and policy (lesson 11). A reviewer then reads the human plan with the flagged items on top.
Only after the review and the checks pass does apply run, using exactly the saved plan, so what was reviewed is what happens.

blocks.md: **The same idea in other IaC tools.** AWS **CloudFormation** (AWS's own IaC service, with templates in JSON or YAML) has **change sets**, which "preview how proposed changes to a stack might impact your running resources", including whether resources will be replaced or deleted ([AWS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/using-cfn-updating-stacks-changesets.html)). **Helm** packages Kubernetes manifests as charts with templates; `helm template` renders a chart locally into plain YAML ([Helm](https://helm.sh/docs/helm/helm_template/)), so you review and scan the manifests that will really be applied, not the templates.

blocks.question: A reviewer reads only the HCL diff in a PR, which changes a variable default from `10.0.0.0/16` to a module input. Why should the pipeline also check the plan JSON?
options: The plan JSON holds the resolved values, such as the CIDR the module actually produces, while the HCL only shows a reference
The HCL diff is always longer
Plan JSON is required by Git
HCL cannot contain security groups
blocks.explain: Values from variables, modules and data sources are only known after planning. Scanning the plan catches what the source hides behind references.

blocks.question: A plan shows `-/+ resource "aws_db_instance" "orders"` after someone renamed a parameter. What should the reviewer conclude?
options: It is a harmless in-place update
Terraform will only update tags
Nothing, because apply asks for confirmation again
The database will be destroyed and recreated, so its data is at risk unless this is intended and backed up
blocks.explain: -/+ is destroy and then create replacement. For a stateful resource that is a data-loss event and needs an explicit decision, not a skim.

lessons.title: Terraform state: the file that holds every secret

blocks.md:
Terraform's **state** is a JSON file that maps each resource in your code to the real object it created, with that object's attributes. HashiCorp's [sensitive data guide](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/manage-sensitive-data) is direct: if you add secret values to your configuration, "Terraform stores those secrets in its state and plan files", and local state is "a plaintext file".

Many people think `sensitive = true` protects a value. It only hides it in CLI output. Here is a real run.

blocks.caption: A variable marked sensitive, passed into a resource. terraform_data is Terraform's built-in resource that just stores values, so this needs no cloud account.

blocks.code:
# terraform_data.db will be created
  + resource "terraform_data" "db" {
      + id     = (known after apply)
      + input  = {
          + engine   = "postgres"
          + password = (sensitive value)
        }
    }

$ grep -n password terraform.tfstate
21:                "password": "correct-horse-42"
27:                  "password": "string"
34:                "password": "correct-horse-42"
40:                  "password": "string"
54:                "value": "password"
blocks.caption: Real output, Terraform 1.7.5. The plan hides the value; the state file stores it in clear text twice. Further down, `sensitive_attributes` records the path, which only tells the CLI what to hide.

blocks.md:
**A real chain from one state file** ([Pen Test Partners, January 2026](https://www.pentestpartners.com/security-blog/compromising-a-multi-cloud-environment-from-a-single-exposed-secret/)), a penetration testing firm reporting an assessment:

1. An S3 bucket's access controls let people who should not see it read Terraform state files.
2. The state held login details for an automated GitHub app.
3. That opened a private repository holding the credentials of a privileged Azure service principal (an identity for software in Azure).
4. The principal could read Azure Key Vault, which held an AWS access key for an administrator role in a separate AWS account.

None of these platforms were connected by design: reused, over-privileged secrets joined them. The firm's conclusion: supporting artefacts such as state files proved as sensitive as production systems.

blocks.title: One readable state bucket, four platforms

scenes.caption: The tester finds an S3 bucket whose policy lets the wrong people read Terraform state.
The state file holds credentials for a GitHub app, which open a private repository.
The repository holds an Azure service principal's secret. The principal reads Key Vault.
Key Vault holds an AWS key for an admin role in a different AWS account. One readable file became admin in a second cloud.

blocks.md:
**Writing state is worse than reading it.** Daniel Grzelak of Plerion showed in February 2024 ([Hacking Terraform state](https://www.plerion.com/blog/hacking-terraform-state-for-privilege-escalation)) what someone who can only edit the state file can do. Adding a fake entry that points at a real resource makes the next plan propose deleting it, hidden in a long plan. Adding an entry that names a provider from the public registry makes `terraform init` download it, and its code runs when Terraform loads it, before anyone is asked to approve an apply. Grzelak's point: control of state is control of the pipeline.

The post's defences: only the deployment pipeline's identity may write state; providers are pre-installed in an immutable runner image, so an unknown one fails; and the plan step runs with a read-only cloud role, so code that runs at plan time cannot change anything.

blocks.caption: Fixed. Remote, encrypted, locked state in its own bucket. The password flows from an ephemeral resource into a write-only argument, used during apply and kept out of plan and state. Providers must support write-only arguments; password_wo is HashiCorp's own example.

blocks.md:
**Locking note.** The S3 backend's `use_lockfile` stores a lock object next to the state; HashiCorp's [S3 backend docs](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/backend/s3) mark DynamoDB-based locking as deprecated. OpenTofu, the open-source Terraform fork, can also encrypt state client-side.

**Defender view.**

- **Prevent**: one state bucket per environment, readable and writable only by the pipeline's roles; versioning on, so a tampered or deleted state can be rolled back; no secrets in configuration where an ephemeral or write-only path exists, or reference secrets by ARN from a secret manager.
- **Detect**: CloudTrail data events on the state bucket (who read or wrote `terraform.tfstate`), and an alert on any principal other than the pipeline; secret scanners run on state files too.
- **Respond**: treat every value in a leaked state as exposed and rotate it; compare the current state with a known-good version before the next apply.

blocks.question: A team marks every secret variable `sensitive = true` and says their state is now safe to share with all engineers. What is wrong?
options: sensitive only redacts CLI and UI output; the values are still in the state file in plain text
Nothing: sensitive values are encrypted in state
sensitive deletes the values after apply
State files never contain variables
blocks.explain: The real run shows the password twice in terraform.tfstate. To keep a value out of state you need ephemeral values or write-only arguments, or a secret manager referenced at runtime.

blocks.question: Grzelak's attack adds a resource that names an attacker's provider to the state. Why does a required manual approval before apply not stop it?
options: Approvals are optional in Terraform
terraform init downloads the provider and Terraform runs its code while planning, before anyone is asked to approve
The provider runs only after apply
State files are not read during plan
blocks.explain: Grzelak notes that even if the reviewer rejects the plan, the code has already executed. That is why the post recommends pre-installed providers in an immutable image and a read-only role for the plan step.

lessons.title: Scanners in the pipeline: Checkov, Trivy and zizmor

blocks.md:
The cloud security course ran Checkov on a Terraform file. This lesson widens the net: the same pipeline should scan every kind of configuration it applies, including its own workflow files, and the team must know what each tool misses.

The tools:

- **Checkov** (open source, created by Bridgecrew, the company behind TerraGoat in lesson 14): static analysis for IaC with more than 750 built-in policies, covering Terraform, Terraform plan JSON, CloudFormation, Kubernetes, Helm and GitHub Actions ([Checkov](https://www.checkov.io/1.Welcome/What%20is%20Checkov.html)).
- **Trivy** (from Aqua Security; pronounced "tri" as in trigger, "vy" as in envy): a scanner for vulnerabilities, secrets and misconfigurations. `trivy config` scans Terraform, CloudFormation, Azure ARM templates, Helm charts, Kubernetes and Dockerfiles ([Trivy](https://trivy.dev/docs/latest/guide/scanner/misconfiguration/)). The older **tfsec** scanner now lives inside Trivy; its repository says "Tfsec is now part of Trivy".
- **zizmor**: static analysis for GitHub Actions workflows, from lesson 7.
**CloudFormation.** A template that switches off all four Block Public Access settings on a bucket:
