blocks.title: Findings per tool and input (real runs in this lesson)

scenes.caption: Checkov on the CloudFormation bucket: 6 failed checks, 4 of them about public access.
On the risky workflow, Checkov reports 2 findings and zizmor 5 (plus 4 suppressed as low confidence). Different tools, different blind spots.
Checkov on the lesson 8 plan JSON: 2 findings, both on the open security group. Neither built-in check noticed the wildcard OIDC trust; that needs a custom rule (lesson 11).

blocks.md:
**Scan the plan, not only the source.** Checkov's docs show the plan workflow: `terraform show -json tfplan.binary > tfplan.json` then `checkov -f tfplan.json` ([Checkov plan scanning](https://www.checkov.io/7.Scan%20Examples/Terraform%20Plan%20Scanning.html)). On the lesson 8 plan it reported CKV_AWS_24 ("Ensure no security groups allow ingress from 0.0.0.0:0 to port 22") and CKV2_AWS_5 (security group not attached to anything). The plan has resolved values that the source hides behind variables and modules.

**Suppressions must carry a reason.** Checkov reads inline comments of the form `#checkov:skip=CKV_AWS_20:The bucket is a public static content host` ([suppressions](https://www.checkov.io/2.Basics/Suppressing%20and%20Skipping%20Policies.html)). Require that every skip names the check and says why, and review new skips like code, because a skip is a policy exception.

No scanner knows your organisation's rules. Built-in checks catch common misconfigurations; rules such as "deploy roles must trust one exact environment" need policy you write yourself. Run several scanners, rank by exposure, and fill the gaps with policy as code. Scanners are third-party code too: in March 2026 most trivy-action tags were force-pushed to a credential stealer (CVE-2026-33634). Pin them by SHA and run them in jobs with no secrets.

blocks.question: Checkov passes a workflow that uses pull_request_target and checks out the PR head commit, while zizmor fails it. What is the right conclusion?
options: Checkov is broken and should be removed
The workflow is safe because one scanner passed it
Tools have different rule sets; run a workflow-specific analyser alongside a general IaC scanner, and treat a pass as "no known pattern found", not "safe"
zizmor is wrong, because pull_request_target is required for forks
blocks.explain: In the real run only zizmor's dangerous-triggers audit flagged the pwn request. A clean scan only means no rule matched.

blocks.question: A developer adds `#checkov:skip=CKV_AWS_24` with no comment to silence the open-SSH finding. What should the pipeline enforce?
options: Nothing: skips are always fine
Delete all skip comments automatically
Disable CKV_AWS_24 everywhere
Skips must name a reason (and ideally an owner and an end date) and go through review like any exception
blocks.explain: Checkov's format includes a suppression comment after the check id. A skip without a reason is an unreviewed exception to policy.

lessons.title: Policy as code with OPA and Rego

blocks.md:
**Policy as code** means writing rules as files that a program evaluates, kept in version control, reviewed, and tested like any code. The same rule can then run in a developer's terminal, in CI, and at deploy time, and every decision can be traced to a commit.

The **Open Policy Agent** (OPA, pronounced "oh-pa") is "an open source, general-purpose policy engine", a graduated project of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) ([OPA docs](https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs)). It decouples the decision from enforcement: your pipeline asks OPA a question with JSON input, and OPA answers from policy. Policies are written in **Rego** (pronounced "ray-go"), a declarative language that OPA's docs say "was inspired by Datalog", a logic query language.

Four ideas cover most of Rego:

- `deny contains msg if { ... }` adds `msg` to a set called `deny` whenever every line in the body is true.
- Lines in one body are joined by AND. Two rules with the same name are joined by OR: each adds its own messages.
- `some x in collection` tries every element; the rule fires for each element that makes all lines true.
- `not expr` is true when the expression is false or undefined, which is how you test that something is missing.

The input here is the plan JSON from lesson 8, the format OPA's [Terraform guide](https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/terraform) uses.

blocks.code:
package terraform.guardrails

import rego.v1

# Rule 1: no SSH (port 22) open to the whole internet
deny contains msg if {
	some rc in input.resource_changes
	rc.type == "aws_security_group"
	some rule in rc.change.after.ingress
	rule.from_port <= 22
	rule.to_port >= 22
	"0.0.0.0/0" in rule.cidr_blocks
	msg := sprintf("%s: SSH open to 0.0.0.0/0", [rc.address])
}

# Rule 2: a role trusting GitHub OIDC must name an exact subject
deny contains msg if {
	some rc in input.resource_changes
	rc.type == "aws_iam_role"
	doc := json.unmarshal(rc.change.after.assume_role_policy)
	some st in doc.Statement
	endswith(st.Principal.Federated, "token.actions.githubusercontent.com")
	not st.Condition.StringEquals["token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub"]
	msg := sprintf("%s: GitHub OIDC trust without an exact sub", [rc.address])
}
blocks.caption: Rule 2 is the one no built-in scanner caught: it parses the trust policy, stored in the plan as a JSON string. Rule 1 is a first draft: it misses protocol "-1" (all traffic, ports 0 to 0), IPv6 ::/0 and separate aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule resources.

blocks.title: Rule 1 evaluated against the lesson 8 plan
blocks.code:
package terraform.guardrails

import rego.v1

# Rule 1: no SSH (port 22) open to the whole internet
deny contains msg if {
	some rc in input.resource_changes
	rc.type == "aws_security_group"
	some rule in rc.change.after.ingress
	rule.from_port <= 22
	rule.to_port >= 22
	"0.0.0.0/0" in rule.cidr_blocks
	msg := sprintf("%s: SSH open to 0.0.0.0/0", [rc.address])
}

# Rule 2: a role trusting GitHub OIDC must name an exact subject
deny contains msg if {
	some rc in input.resource_changes
	rc.type == "aws_iam_role"
	doc := json.unmarshal(rc.change.after.assume_role_policy)
	some st in doc.Statement
	endswith(st.Principal.Federated, "token.actions.githubusercontent.com")
	not st.Condition.StringEquals["token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub"]
	msg := sprintf("%s: GitHub OIDC trust without an exact sub", [rc.address])
}

scenes.caption: OPA tries each element of resource_changes. The first is the IAM role.
Its type is not aws_security_group, so this attempt fails and no message is added.
Next element: the security group. The type line is now true.
It iterates over the group's ingress rules. There is one, for port 22.
22 <= 22 and 22 >= 22: port 22 is inside the range.
0.0.0.0/0 is in cidr_blocks, so every line is true and a message joins the deny set.

blocks.caption: Real results of querying data.terraform.guardrails.deny on both plans, evaluated with rego-cpp 1.5.2 (Microsoft's Rego interpreter, through its Python binding). `opa eval` takes the same policy and the same query.

blocks.prompt: Rule 2 fires when there is no StringEquals entry for the sub. Suppose a role uses `StringLike` with an exact value and no wildcard, `repo:example-org/shop-site:environment:production`. What does rule 2 do, and is that right?
blocks.reveal:
It fires, because the `not st.Condition.StringEquals[...]` line is true: there is no StringEquals key for the sub. The role is actually safe (a StringLike pattern with no `*` or `?` matches only itself), so this is a **false positive**.

That is normal for a first policy. Either refine the rule (also accept StringLike values that contain no wildcard characters) or keep it strict on purpose and tell teams to use StringEquals. Both are fine; what matters is that the choice is written down, tested and reviewed, which is the point of policy as code.

blocks.md:
**Running it in CI.** **Conftest**, maintained in the Open Policy Agent GitHub organisation, is a tool for testing structured configuration such as Kubernetes YAML or Terraform plans against Rego. It looks for rules named `deny`, `violation` and `warn` in a `policy` directory by default, but only in the package `main` ([Conftest](https://www.conftest.dev/)). The policy above is `package terraform.guardrails`, so it runs with `conftest test --namespace terraform.guardrails tfplan.json`; a plain `conftest test` would find no rules and pass everything. Its report counts `deny` results as failures, which fail the job, and `warn` results as warnings.

**Testing the policy.** OPA treats rules whose names start with `test_` as unit tests, run with `opa test` ([policy testing](https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/policy-testing)). A test feeds a tiny input with `with input as` and checks the result:

blocks.caption: Unit tests for rule 1, in the form `opa test` runs. The two cases match evaluating the policy directly on the same inputs: the open group gives one deny (count 1) and the 10.0.0.0/16 group none (count 0).

blocks.question: In Rego, a rule body has five lines. Four are true for a resource and one is false. What happens?
options: The rule does not fire for that resource, because lines in a body are joined by AND
The rule fires, since most lines are true
Rego raises an error
The rule fires once for each true line
blocks.explain: All lines in a body must hold for the same choice of variables. To express OR, write a second rule with the same name.

blocks.question: Why pass the plan JSON to OPA rather than the raw HCL files?
options: OPA cannot read text files
The plan JSON contains resolved values and each resource's planned actions, so policy judges what will actually happen
HCL is not allowed in CI
The plan JSON is smaller
blocks.explain: OPA's Terraform guide works on the plan JSON because it shows resource_changes with resolved attributes and actions such as create or delete.

lessons.title: Sentinel, enforcement levels and guardrails developers accept

blocks.md:
A policy that blocks every pull request on day one gets switched off by day three. The hard part of policy as code is not writing rules but rolling them out so teams keep shipping. This lesson covers HashiCorp's Sentinel, its enforcement levels, and how to apply the same ideas with OPA.

**HCP Terraform** is HashiCorp's managed service for running Terraform (HCP stands for HashiCorp Cloud Platform). It checks every run's plan against **policy sets** before apply, written in one of three frameworks: **Sentinel** (HashiCorp's own policy language), **OPA**, or a native HCL-based **Terraform policy** framework that needs Terraform 1.17 or later ([policy enforcement](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cloud-docs/policy-enforcement)).

blocks.caption: The lesson 11 rule 1 in Sentinel, built from HashiCorp's tfplan/v2 import, filter, any, contains and is empty documentation. Run it with the Sentinel CLI against a mocked plan, or in HCP Terraform.

blocks.md:
Read it like Rego. `filter` keeps elements of a collection whose body is true; `any` is true if the body holds for at least one element; `contains` tests membership. The policy passes when `main` is true, so it passes when no offending group exists.

**Enforcement levels** are where Sentinel shines: the level is set when the policy is deployed, not inside the policy, so the same rule can warn in one place and block in another ([enforcement levels](https://developer.hashicorp.com/sentinel/docs/concepts/enforcement-levels)):

- **Advisory** (the default): the policy may fail; a warning is shown or logged.
- **Soft mandatory**: the policy must pass unless someone with permission overrides it. HashiCorp notes this gives privilege separation and non-repudiation, because the person who overrode a failed policy is recorded.
- **Hard mandatory**: the policy must pass no matter what; the only way around it is removing the policy.

blocks.title: Where policy runs, from fastest feedback to last line of defence

scenes.caption: The earliest check is on the developer's machine: the same Rego or scanner, run before pushing, with results in seconds.
In the pull request, scanners and conftest comment on the exact lines. This is where most findings should be fixed.
At plan time, policy sets in HCP Terraform (or conftest in your own pipeline) judge the resolved plan, with an enforcement level per rule.
Cloud guardrails such as AWS service control policies deny forbidden actions even if a change skips the pipeline entirely.
Drift and posture scans catch what still gets through: console changes and old resources (lesson 13).

blocks.md:
**A rollout that keeps developers on side**, using these levels:

1. **Start advisory.** Run a new rule as a warning for a while and count what it would block. Fix the rule's false positives (like lesson 11's StringLike case) before anyone is blocked.
2. **Promote by impact.** Make a small set of rules hard mandatory: internet-exposed admin ports, public data, wildcard trust on deploy roles. Make the long tail soft mandatory, with a recorded override.
3. **Write the fix into the message.** "SSH open to 0.0.0.0/0: use the bastion module or restrict cidr_blocks" is a guardrail; "policy failed" is a wall.
4. **Make exceptions code.** Each exception names the resource, an owner, a reason and an end date, lives in the policy repository and is reviewed. When it expires, the rule applies again by itself.
5. **Offer a paved road.** A shared Terraform module that is secure by default means most teams never meet the rule.

blocks.caption: Exceptions as reviewed data in Rego. An exception downgrades a deny to a warn until its end date. The pipeline passes today's date in the input, so tests can pin any date.

blocks.code:
# input: three groups open to SSH, today = 2026-11-14
deny: ["aws_security_group.legacy: SSH open to 0.0.0.0/0",
       "aws_security_group.web: SSH open to 0.0.0.0/0"]
warn: ["aws_security_group.bastion: allowed by exception until 2026-12-31"]
blocks.caption: Real results (rego-cpp 1.5.2). bastion's exception is still valid, so it only warns; legacy's expired on 2026-06-30, so it is denied again with no one having to remember; web never had one.

blocks.question: A new rule would block 40 pull requests a week across the company, and nobody has seen its results yet. Which enforcement level should it start at?
options: Hard mandatory, so the problem is fixed fastest
Advisory, to measure impact and fix false positives before anything blocks
Soft mandatory with no override permission
No policy at all
blocks.explain: Advisory is Sentinel's default and lets a policy fail with a warning. Starting there turns the unknown 40 a week into a measured list before teams are blocked.

blocks.question: Why does a soft-mandatory override help security even though it lets a failing change through?
options: It does not; overrides are always a weakness
Overrides fix the underlying problem automatically
Soft-mandatory policies are evaluated twice
It records who chose to override a failed policy, giving non-repudiation and a reviewable trail, instead of people disabling the policy quietly
blocks.explain: HashiCorp's docs say the override provides privilege separation and non-repudiation, since the primary actor explicitly overrode a failed policy. A visible, attributed exception beats a removed rule.

lessons.title: Drift detection: when the cloud stops matching the code

blocks.md:
All the checks so far run on changes that go through the pipeline. Some changes do not. During an incident an engineer opens a port in the console; an old script tags a bucket public. The cloud security course called this **drift**: the live state no longer matches the code. Here is how to detect it and what to do next.

HashiCorp separates two kinds ([HCP Terraform health](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cloud-docs/workspaces/health)): **configuration drift**, where an outside change makes reality disagree with your configuration (the opened port), and **state drift**, where an outside change does not contradict the configuration (for example an attribute you never set). Configuration drift is what security cares about.

**The simplest detector is a scheduled plan.** `terraform plan` refreshes state from the live cloud by default, so if anything changed outside Terraform, the plan proposes changing it back. With `-detailed-exitcode` the exit code says which ([terraform plan](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan)): **0** succeeded with no changes, **1** error, **2** succeeded with changes present. On a branch nobody is editing, 2 means drift.

A local test with the hashicorp/local provider (a file stands in for a cloud object): `plan -detailed-exitcode` returned 0 after apply; after editing the managed file by hand, it returned 2.

blocks.code:
name: drift-check
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "17 3 * * *"              # every night at 03:17 UTC
permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write
jobs:
  drift:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@e1253824e5c10ff9df46874f81ed3ec929e19cfd # v6.3.0
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/shop-plan-readonly
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@dfe3c3f87815947d99a8997f908cb6525fc44e9e # v4.0.1
        with:
          terraform_wrapper: false
      - run: terraform init -input=false
      - name: Compare the live cloud with the code
        run: |
          set +e
          terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -input=false -lock=false -no-color > drift.txt
          code=$?
          set -e
          case "$code" in
            0) echo "No drift" ;;
            2) echo "Drift found"; cat drift.txt; exit 1 ;;
            *) echo "Plan failed"; exit 1 ;;
          esac
blocks.caption: A nightly drift job. It uses the read-only plan role (it never needs to change anything), skips the state lock because that role cannot write, and fails on exit code 2 so the owners are alerted.

blocks.title: How long a console change stays open: nightly vs weekly checks

scenes.caption: Hour 0: the pipeline applies reviewed code. Nightly drift checks run at 03:17 each day (hours 3, 27, 51, 75).
Hour 82: someone opens SSH to 0.0.0.0/0 in the console while debugging. No pull request, no scan.
Nightly: the hour-99 run exits 2 and alerts. The port was open for 17 hours.
Weekly (one run, at hour 147): the same change is found 65 hours after it was made. Detection delay is a setting you choose.

blocks.md:
**Other detectors.** AWS CloudFormation has built-in drift detection for stacks: each resource gets a status such as IN_SYNC, MODIFIED, DELETED or NOT_CHECKED, and a stack is DRIFTED if any resource has drifted ([AWS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/using-cfn-stack-drift.html)). HCP Terraform runs scheduled **health assessments** that show drifted resources per workspace. A plan only sees what Terraform manages: a rule added in the console as a new object is invisible to it. Posture tools (CSPM) cover those.

**Responding to drift: revert or codify.**

- **Revert**: the change was wrong (the open port). Apply the code again, then find out who made the change and why, from CloudTrail.
- **Codify**: the change was right (an emergency fix). Put it into the code through a normal pull request. Terraform's **refresh-only** mode (`terraform plan -refresh-only`) exists for this: its docs mention changing remote objects "while responding to an incident", then reconciling state without changing anything.

Do not "fix" drift by blindly running apply from the drift job. The job holds a read-only role on purpose, and an automatic revert can undo an emergency change in the middle of an incident. Alert, decide, then go through the normal pipeline.

blocks.question: A scheduled `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` on main returns 2. Nobody merged anything since the last apply. What does it most likely mean?
options: Terraform crashed
No changes are needed
Something changed outside Terraform: drift that the owners must review
The state file is encrypted
blocks.explain: Exit code 2 means the plan succeeded and has changes. With no new code, those changes come from the live side: drift. Exit code 1 would be an error.

blocks.question: During an outage an engineer raised a database's connection limit in the console, and the fix should stay. What is the right drift response?
options: Run apply to revert it, since code is the source of truth
Codify it: change the Terraform code through a pull request to match, using refresh-only planning to reconcile state, so the next apply does not undo it
Delete the database from state
Ignore the drift alerts from now on
blocks.explain: This is the codify path. Reverting would reintroduce the outage; ignoring trains everyone to ignore drift alerts.

lessons.title: Putting it together: a secure pipeline, a response plan, practice

blocks.md:
Here is the whole course as one Terraform pipeline for one repository. Each line names the lesson where it was taught.

- **Pull request** (untrusted): `pull_request` trigger, `permissions: {}` then `contents: read`, GitHub-hosted runner, egress allowlist (3). zizmor on workflows, Checkov on IaC (10). Plan with a **read-only** role trusted for `repo:ORG/REPO:pull_request` and, for the nightly drift job, `repo:ORG/REPO:ref:refs/heads/main` (6, 9), then scan the plan JSON and run conftest policy (8, 11). No caches written for release (7).
- **Apply** (trusted): push to main, job in the `production` environment with required reviewers, prevent self-review and a main-only branch rule (2, 4). Apply role trusts `environment:production` exactly (6). Apply the saved, reviewed plan (8).
- **State**: dedicated encrypted bucket, versioned, writable only by the apply role; secrets kept out of state with ephemeral values and write-only arguments (9).
- **After**: nightly drift check with the read-only role (13); policy exceptions with end dates (12).

blocks.title: The finished pipeline: two roles, one gate, one state

scenes.caption: A pull request runs on a clean hosted runner with no secrets. Scanners and policy read the code and the plan JSON.
The plan role can only read, so PR code that runs during plan (lesson 9) cannot change the cloud. It can still read the state and every secret in it, which is why secrets stay out of state.
After merge, the apply job waits at the production environment until a second person approves.
Only a job admitted to the environment can assume the apply role. It applies the reviewed plan and writes state.
Every night the drift job compares the cloud with main using the read-only role, and alerts on exit code 2.

blocks.md:
**When a pipeline is compromised: a response plan.** The cases in this course give the steps.

1. **Contain**: disable the affected workflows; take self-hosted runners offline and rebuild them from a clean image (PyTorch).
2. **Rotate everything the pipeline could read**: secrets at every level, registry tokens, cloud keys, personal access tokens, deploy keys (PyPI after Ultralytics, CircleCI to its customers). GITHUB_TOKENs expire with the job; OIDC roles need only their trust reviewed.
3. **Find what was published or changed**: releases, packages and images built in the window (yank or delete bad ones), commits and tags, cache entries (delete them), and the Terraform state (compare with a known-good version before the next apply).
4. **Scope with logs**: the platform's audit log, workflow run logs, cloud audit logs for each credential from the start of the window, outbound connections from runners.
5. **Fix the root cause**, then add a detection for it: a zizmor or Checkov rule, a policy, an egress allowlist.

The question to ask of every part of a pipeline: who can change what this runs, and what can it reach when it does? If the answer to the first is "anyone who can open a PR" and to the second is "production", there is a gap, however many scanners run.

**Practice legally.** Work only on systems you own or have written permission to test.

- [CI/CD Goat](https://github.com/cider-security-research/cicd-goat): "a deliberately vulnerable CI/CD environment" with challenges, run locally in Docker.
- [TerraGoat](https://github.com/bridgecrewio/terragoat): Bridgecrew's "Vulnerable by Design" Terraform repository. Scan it with Checkov or Trivy and write Rego for what they miss; it is not necessary to deploy it.
- Run [zizmor](https://docs.zizmor.sh/) on your own repositories' workflows and fix what it finds.
- Read GitHub Security Lab's [preventing pwn requests](https://securitylab.github.com/resources/github-actions-preventing-pwn-requests/) and OWASP's [CI/CD Top 10](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-ci-cd-security-risks/), then map each risk to a control in your own pipeline.

blocks.question: In the finished pipeline, why do pull requests get a separate read-only plan role instead of the apply role?
options: PR code is untrusted and plan can run provider or PR-controlled code; a read-only role means that code cannot change the cloud even if it runs
Read-only roles are faster
The apply role cannot run terraform plan
GitHub forbids write roles on pull requests
blocks.explain: Lessons 2 and 9: anything that runs during a PR may be attacker-controlled. Giving it only read access caps the damage, while reviewers still see a real plan.

blocks.question: A self-hosted runner is suspected of running attacker code. What is the right first containment step?
options: Delete suspicious files on it and keep using it
Take it offline and replace it from a clean image, then rotate every secret jobs on it could reach
Restart the runner service
Rename the runner
blocks.explain: A persistent runner can hide leftover processes and modified tools (the PyTorch case). Rebuilding from a known-good image is the only state you can trust; secrets that passed through it must be treated as stolen.

blocks.question: Which of these is still a gap in the finished pipeline, and needs a different control?
options: A PR that edits the Makefile to steal secrets
An engineer opening a port in the console during an incident
A tampered pip cache restored by the release job
A wildcard OIDC trust on the apply role
blocks.explain: The first, third and fourth are handled inside the pipeline (no secrets on PRs, no release caches, an exact environment trust checked by policy). Console changes skip the pipeline; drift detection, and cloud guardrails that limit who may change security groups, are the controls for them.
